corrections.compiler_and_flags: z-fasta 0.3.5 built with Zig 0.16.0, `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dstrip=true`; build.zig uses standardTargetOptions and no -Dtarget/-Dcpu is passed, so the binary targets the host (native) CPU. samtools 1.24 and HTSlib 1.24 built from source by tools/install.sh with plain `./configure` and `make`, i.e. package-default flags (htslib Makefile `-g -Wall -O2 -fvisibility=hidden`, samtools Makefile `-g -Wall -O2`) for generic x86-64; C compiler not named.
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (README Performance section); Linux x86_64 (glibc 2.43 target in the report provenance); zebrac 0.6.2, 5 measured samples after 3 warmups, 5000 ms budget per command, warm cache.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 9 stars, 0 forks (GitHub repo page, 2026-10-11); new project (v0.3.5, 244 commits).
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark with the author's own runner and reports. Both sides are single-threaded (no threads in src/indexer.zig; HTSlib's fai_build_core is a per-character bgzf_getc loop), so the gap is algorithmic: z-fasta validates fixed-width line blocks with SIMD whitespace counts over 256 KiB reads. The cross-tool `--emit-fai` lane constructs the .fai bytes but discards the emitted stream while samtools writes a .fai sidecar file, so output destinations differ (REPORT.md says so). z-fasta is built for the native CPU while samtools uses its package-default -O2 generic build; the C compiler is unnamed. The 7.9 GiB/s genome throughput is a warm page-cache figure. The rust-bio lane is a custom FAI writer, not a rust-bio command. v0.3.5 indexing is 10-40% slower than v0.3.4 on 15 of 30 cases (genome .fai 382.4 ms vs 321.2 ms) after whitespace validation was added. FAI parity with samtools passed 20/20 structural edge cases.
corrections.why_faster: From the sources: z-fasta's indexer (src/indexer.zig) checks expected line terminators at a fixed stride and verifies each 256-line block with a vectorised whitespace count (@Vector, std.simd), reading 256 KiB chunks; HTSlib's fai_build_core reads one character at a time through bgzf_getc and a state machine. Both are single-threaded; the win is the SIMD block-validation algorithm, not a Zig codegen effect.

notes: Numbers verified on README and bench/index/REPORT.md (Table 3 and Table 5). Shortcomings to record: first-party; samtools at package-default -O2 generic x86-64 versus z-fasta built for the native CPU, C compiler unnamed; emit-fai lane discards output while peers write files; warm cache only. Not a language-level claim.

The win is an algorithm change (hash versus sort), not a language effect. The author's table also measures huniq 2.7.0 (6m04.595s count), runiq and sortuniq. GPL-3.0-or-later.

notes: Numbers match PERFORMANCE.md; added the sorted-report ratio and thread counts. tier_reason: First-party readme table produced by the public benchmark.sh, but no CPU, compiler versions or tool versions are stated and the measured huniq version is not named, so it falls short of A.

corrections.baseline: GNU `sort -u` (uniq mode) and `sort | uniq -c` (count mode), awk (`!visited[$0]++` / associative count), GNU datamash (`-s groupby`), and the author's earlier C++ huniq version 1 (SoftwearDevelopment/huniq: std::getline on std::cin, tsl::sparse_set of 128-bit MetroHash128 values, tsl::sparse_map<std::string,size_t> for counts).
corrections.claimed_speedup: readme.md tables (seconds / peak KB), input = /usr/share/dict/* repeated N times. Uniq mode (the 'shell' lane is `sort -u` per benchmark.sh, not `sort | uniq`): 1 repetition huniq2-rust 0.26 s vs huniq1-c++ 1.67 s, awk 1.63 s, datamash 1.78 s, sort -u 7.30 s; 100 repetitions 43.65 s vs 154.99 s (C++), 239.66 s (awk), 285.94 s (datamash), 1062.07 s (sort -u). Count mode (shell = `sort | uniq -c`), 100 repetitions: 90.80 s vs 150.41 s (C++), 163.13 s (awk), 322.70 s (datamash), 933.67 s. README: 'beats the C++ implementation by a factor of between 6.5 ... and 3.5', 'Compared to sort -u: huniq is around 30 times faster' (28x at 1 repetition, 24x at 100, derived from page data), count mode 'between 25% and 50% faster than the C++ implementation and between 5x and 10x faster than sort | uniq -c'. Memory: about 29.5 MB vs 26.2 MB (C++) in uniq mode, 132 MB vs 60 MB in count mode.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: `cargo build --release` with `[profile.release] lto = "fat"` (Cargo.toml; ahash 0.7, bstr 0.2, clap 3); the C++ version 1 is built by benchmark.sh with its Makefile default `CXXFLAGS ?= -O3`, `-std=c++11`; compiler versions not stated.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 265 stars, 12 forks (GitHub repo page, 2026-10-11); crates.io huniq 2.7.0 (2022-04-20), 354,765 downloads (59,268 recent).
corrections.caveats: Author-run with no machine, compiler or tool versions stated, and the huniq version measured is not named; benchmark.sh loops until aborted and times each tool with `time` while a shell loop cats /usr/share/dict/* into it, so the producer can bound the fastest lanes. Uniq mode stores only 64-bit ahash values (128-bit MetroHash in v1), so collisions can drop lines. The C++ comparator is the author's own v1 built at -O3 but reading with std::getline on std::cin without sync_with_stdio(false) and using the memory-optimised tsl::sparse_set/sparse_map, so the 3.5x to 6.5x reflects I/O and hash-table choices rather than Rust versus C++. Hash versus sort is an algorithm difference. Licence BSD-3-Clause per Cargo.toml and the readme text; GitHub detects no LICENSE file. A competitor's table (cuniq PERFORMANCE.md) measured huniq 2.7.0 at 6m04.595s on a 32 GiB file against 14m11.935s for `sort -u | wc -l`.
corrections.why_faster: Versus sort: hash set instead of sorting (readme). Versus the author's C++ v1 (from the sources): v1 reads lines with std::getline on synced std::cin and inserts into tsl::sparse_set (128-bit MetroHash128) or tsl::sparse_map<std::string,size_t>; v2 reads locked byte records through bstr without UTF-8 validation, inserts 64-bit ahash values into a hashbrown HashSet with an identity hasher (HashMap<Vec<u8>,u64> with ahash for counts) and mem::forget()s the table at exit. I/O path and hash-table library, not compiler codegen.

notes: Numbers match the readme; corrected the uniq-mode 'shell' lane to `sort -u` (benchmark.sh meas_shell). Shortcomings to record: no hardware, compiler or version info; producer-bound pipeline harness; C++ comparator is the author's own v1 with synced iostreams and tsl::sparse_set (C++ side at -O3); 64-bit hash-only dedup. maintenance stale (last commit 2024-01-26).
